prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform a lumbar puncture while the posterior fossa lesion compresses the fourth ventricle
Do not attribute the unresponsiveness and quadriparesis to residual anaesthesia or sedation
Do not start corticosteroids before tissue has been obtained, except dexamethasone for hydrocephalus or impending herniation after neurosurgical discussion
Do not resect the lesion or start radiotherapy or chemotherapy on the imaging appearance alone
Do not diagnose MS based on non-specific white-matter lesions alone without meeting the 2024 revised McDonald criteria and excluding mimics
Do not start teriflunomide in a woman of child-bearing potential without effective contraception (teratogenic, long elimination half-life)
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as maintenance treatment for MS: they do not prevent relapses or disability and cause cumulative harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation of B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)
Do not omit spinal cord MRI in a patient with myelopathic signs even if the brain MRI alone meets DIS: cord lesions count toward DIS and separate MS from NMOSD
required_recommendations: State relapsing-remitting MS by the 2024 McDonald criteria, naming the regions that give DIS and, where needed, what gives DIT or positive CSF (here infratentorial, cortical-juxtacortical, periventricular and spinal cord, with histology excluding lymphoma and glioma).

Manage in intensive care: protect the airway (GCS 8 with a medullary lesion; intubate if airway protection or ventilation fails), keep nil by mouth until swallowing is assessed, and monitor for hydrocephalus with neurosurgical review.
Obtain urgent stereotactic biopsy of the right temporal lesion before corticosteroids; give dexamethasone only for hydrocephalus or impending herniation, after neurosurgical discussion.
Once histology shows demyelination, give IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days, and start plasma exchange early if there is no clear improvement given the severity of the attack.

Stop metformin and glibenclamide while she is nil by mouth and on high-dose steroids, and control glucose with variable-rate intravenous insulin and frequent capillary glucose; plan for hypoglycaemia risk if glibenclamide is restarted after the pulse.

Offer disease-modifying therapy after diagnosis, choosing efficacy by disease activity (a severe multifocal tumefactive attack after two earlier episodes: a high-efficacy therapy is appropriate), after discussing pregnancy plans and contraception.

Before starting disease-modifying therapy, screen HBsAg, anti-HBc, HCV, HIV (done) and VZV IgG, add anti-JCV antibodies if natalizumab is considered, and give any live vaccine at least 4-6 weeks before starting.

avoided_actions.rationale: A 3.8 cm posterior fossa lesion compressing the fourth ventricle in a patient with GCS 8 makes lumbar puncture unsafe because of the risk of tonsillar herniation.
The MRI shows mass-like lesions with open-ring enhancement, not an embolic infarct pattern; there is no cardiac source question.
Postoperative sinus tachycardia only, with no rhythm question; monitoring adds nothing to the diagnosis.

differential.key_features: Raised by multifocal enhancing lesions; the steroid-free biopsy shows active demyelination with only reactive B cells and negative EBER; HIV negative.
Biopsy shows demyelination without atypical glial cells, mitoses, microvascular proliferation or necrosis; open rings, Cho/NAA 1.17 without lipid, and several separate lesions argue against it.
A three-week prodrome before surgery; lesions are expansile with open-ring enhancement and only leading-edge restricted diffusion, not a vascular territory infarct; no intraoperative hypotension.
Spine MRI shows only a short non-enhancing dorsolateral C3-C4 lesion, and cord infarction would not explain the reduced consciousness or the brain lesions.
Afebrile; CRP and leukocytosis fit the recent laparotomy; restriction is at the leading edge rather than the core; histology without organisms.

AQP4-IgG negative by cell-based assay; short dorsolateral cord lesion; no documented optic neuritis or area postrema syndrome. The absent oligoclonal bands do not count against NMOSD, so the CBA result carries the exclusion.

MOG-IgG negative by live cell-based assay, although large brainstem lesions and absent bands would fit; a non-enhancing periventricular lesion and earlier episodes point to relapsing disease with lesions of different age.
Reduced consciousness is explained by the brainstem lesion; two earlier episodes and non-enhancing older lesions argue against a monophasic illness.
Glucose 188 mg/dL and sodium 139 mEq/L; metabolic causes do not produce focal brainstem and cord lesions.
No witnessed seizure; quadriparesis, areflexia and Babinski signs localise to the brainstem and cord; an EEG, if done, shows diffuse slowing without seizures.

key_clinical_evidence: Unresponsiveness (GCS 8) with flaccid quadriparesis, lower-limb areflexia and bilateral Babinski signs after a three-week prodrome of unsteadiness, slurred speech and dysphagia, from a 3.8 cm left middle cerebellar peduncle, pontine and medullary lesion with open-ring enhancement.
Earlier episodes: bilateral leg numbness for 5 days 2 years ago and right-eye blurring for 3 days 8 months ago, both attributed to other causes and resolved.

DIS: 4 of 5 regions: infratentorial (left middle cerebellar peduncle, pons, medulla), cortical-juxtacortical (right temporal), periventricular (right frontal horn), spinal cord (C3-C4). Four regions establish DIS without a separate DIT; enhancing and non-enhancing lesions coexist.
Stereotactic biopsy of the right temporal lesion: active demyelination with myelin-laden macrophages and preserved axons; no atypical lymphoid or glial cells.
AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG negative by cell-based assay: against NMOSD and MOGAD.
The fourth ventricular compression with GCS 8 makes lumbar puncture unsafe; the diagnosis rests on MRI, serology and tissue.

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Priya Krishnamurthy is a 34-year-old right-handed woman who was transferred to the intensive care unit approximately 6 hours following an otherwise uneventful exploratory laparotomy performed under general anesthesia for evaluation of recurrent right upper quadrant abdominal pain suspected to be related to chronic cholecystitis. The surgical procedure lasted approximately 90 minutes and was reported as uncomplicated, with stable hemodynamics throughout and no episodes of hypotension or hypoxia noted on the anesthesia record. In the post-anesthesia care unit, the nursing staff noted that the patient was not recovering consciousness as expected. She was noted to have no purposeful movement of any extremity, was making only incomprehensible sounds, and was not following commands. The surgical team initially attributed the findings to prolonged effects of general anesthesia, but after 3 hours without improvement, a neurology consultation was requested. On evaluation by the neurology team, the patient was found to have a Glasgow Coma Scale of 8, profound quadriparesis with only trace movement in the upper extremities and no movement in the lower extremities, absent deep tendon reflexes in the lower extremities, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Her preoperative assessment recorded her as conversant and walking independently. On direct questioning, her husband reports that for about three weeks before surgery she had been unsteady on her feet, at times slurred her words and had some difficulty swallowing solids; the family attributed this to her abdominal illness and poor oral intake, and it was not mentioned at the preoperative visit. Her medical history is notable for type 2 diabetes managed with metformin and glibenclamide, and hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. A review of her medical records reveals a prior episode of bilateral lower extremity numbness approximately 2 years ago that lasted 5 days and was attributed to lumbar radiculopathy, and an episode of transient blurry vision in the right eye 8 months ago attributed to dry eye. Both episodes resolved spontaneously.
